overview: Brunei is a continuing sultanate on northern Borneo whose maritime influence once reached far beyond its present territory. This record begins in 1650, long after its emergence, and follows changing sovereignty through British protection to independence. The imported outlines barely change from 1650 to 2020, concealing major territorial losses; they cannot reconstruct the old sultanate’s reach. A different modern outline appears after 2020.

periods.title: A contracting sultanate
periods.summary: Regional authority weakened as European expansion reduced Brunei’s territory.

periods.title: British protection and constitutional change
periods.summary: A protectorate developed into a Resident system, followed by internal self-government.

items.text: A royal genealogy describes a civil war between Sultan Abdul Mubin and Sultan Muhyiuddin. An added manuscript note dates Muhammad Ali’s killing to 4 February 1662. The defeated faction’s wealthy families survived: political defeat did not erase an entire community.

Brunei became a British protectorate in 1888. From 1906, a British Resident advised the sultan in most affairs, with exceptions for Malay customs and Islam. The 1959 constitution established internal self-government; a 1971 revision left defence and external affairs outside that internal independence.

Diplomacy could arrive with a bundle of cloth. In a letter of 15 July 1820, Singapore official William Farquhar acknowledged 100 katis of wax from Pengiran Muda Muhammad Alam and sent patterned cotton and handkerchief cloth in return. Named ship captains carried both goods and correspondence between the courts and ports.

War interrupted these longer histories. Allied forces landed around Brunei Bay on 10 June 1945 and took Brunei town from Japanese occupation. Their advance continued toward Seria’s oilfields. Engineers extinguished burning wells and repaired damaged roads and bridges, practical work needed after the fighting.

An armed uprising began on 8 December 1962. The sultan requested British help, and troops secured government buildings, communications and oil installations while suppressing the revolt. This crisis belongs to the contested politics of decolonisation, before Brunei’s later full independence.

The Brunei shipwreck offers an earlier glimpse of maritime commerce. Dating to the late fifteenth century, before this map record begins, it held Chinese blue-and-white ceramics and jars from China, Thailand and Vietnam. Glass bracelets, bronze gongs, metal ingots and cooking pots travelled alongside the fashionable tableware.

Recovering that cargo was a large underwater investigation. After a 1997 survey, archaeologists excavated for three months in 1998 at about 65 metres depth. They recorded roughly 14,000 significant objects. A broken cooking pot can be as useful to this history as a beautiful vase: both were part of the shipment.

Commercial oil was found at Seria in 1929. The first well, S-1, became an industrial landmark; a monument built nearby in 1991 commemorated the field’s billionth barrel. Brunei’s material history includes drilling equipment and petroleum infrastructure as well as royal buildings and old ceramics.

sections.title: A royal book, a baby and learning

items.text: A Malay royal genealogy copied probably in the 1820s uses Jawi, an Arabic-derived script. Gallop quotes its opening in Roman transliteration: “Bahwa inilah silsilah segala raja2”, meaning “This is the genealogy of the rulers”. The numeral 2 marks a repeated word. This is an editor’s transliteration, not a facsimile of the handwriting.

The same manuscript also became a family notebook. Its final birth notice records Abdul Rajad on 22 January 1831, after an earlier draft gave another date. Protective writings for children’s crying and convulsions appear nearby. They preserve parental worries and historical beliefs, not evidence that the charms cured illness.

Brunei’s modern school system expanded in several languages. A Malay-medium primary school opened in 1912, a Chinese school in 1916, and a nongovernment English primary school at Seria in 1931. The ministry records 32 primary schools by 1941. These dates concern school institutions, not the beginning of religious or family learning.

Secondary schooling came later: the first English-medium secondary school opened in 1953, with Malay-medium secondary education following in 1966. The inclusive education policy introduced in 1997 supported pupils with special educational needs in mainstream classrooms through collaboration with specialist teachers.

sections.title: Homes, food and looking after people

items.text: A royal letter from 28 April 1822 reports a severe epidemic. The sultan apologised that requested weights and measures were below standard because the town was suffering. The letter links illness with interrupted skilled work and overseas exchange; it does not identify the disease well enough for a confident modern diagnosis.

Living over water still requires plumbing. A Kampong Ayer pilot housing project completed in 2012 included sewage treatment, a pumping station toward Sungai Kebun, water pipes and firefighting equipment. Its roofed bridges and leisure platforms connected homes and shared spaces. These improvements belong to a named project, not every historic water-village house.

The same new houses used concrete floors and columns with flame-retardant wooden walls. That combination kept wood in the home while addressing fire and structural safety. Kampong Ayer’s built heritage is continually adapted for the people living there, rather than consisting only of buildings preserved unchanged.

Today’s ambuyat begins with starch from the inside of a sago palm and water. Its sticky texture is twirled onto candas, paired bamboo sticks joined at one end, then dipped in sour, spicy cacah. Dinner gives the chopsticks a workout. This is a documented living food tradition, not a dated seventeenth-century menu.

Food also marks family celebrations. Brunei Tourism describes kelupis, glutinous-rice parcels wrapped in nyirik leaves, as refreshments at Bisaya weddings and special occasions. Some versions include dried shrimp or anchovies. The leaf is part of the packaging, making each portion a small edible present once unwrapped.

ending.text: Brunei did not disappear when its territory contracted or British protection ended. It became fully independent on 1 January 1984 and assumed responsibility for its own defence. The sultanate continues; 1650 is merely this map record’s starting point, not its foundation date.
